title: Regulated Delivery, Platforms & Packaging
scopeHtml: Scope: constraint-driven delivery routes (privilege, HIPAA, GDPR, FedRAMP), requirements, lifecycle, platform choice, version pinning, trust boundaries, accelerators and upstream contribution.

questions.promptHtml:
A client sends PHI to Claude. Which setup is acceptable?

  • A. Console/Workbench for convenience
  • B. A BAA-covered configuration (direct API on a HIPAA-enabled org arranged with Anthropic, or Bedrock/Vertex on the partner's HIPAA-eligible account), with logging paths scoped under the same BAA
  • C. A beta feature under the BAA
  • D. Consumer plan with a policy memo

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The BAA does not cover Console, Workbench, beta features or consumer plans; verify feature eligibility.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: PHI may only go to a BAA-covered configuration: a dedicated HIPAA-enabled Anthropic organization (arranged with Anthropic) or Bedrock/Vertex on the partner's HIPAA-eligible account. Any logging or retention path you write to must be scoped under the same BAA. Console, Workbench, beta features and consumer plans are not covered; not every API feature is eligible.

questions.promptHtml:
An EU customer needs data processed only in-region. What is the right route?

  • A. The direct Anthropic API with its default endpoint
  • B. Bedrock or Vertex with the region pinned in client configuration (the direct API does not currently provide EU data residency)
  • C. A global endpoint
  • D. Any region, since data is encrypted

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Defaulting to a global endpoint without a region is the common failure.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Residency must be enforceable in code: pin the region in the client configuration for a covered jurisdiction. The direct Anthropic API does not currently provide EU data residency, and a global endpoint can serve a request from outside the boundary. Encryption (D) does not change where processing happens.

questions.promptHtml:
Which is NOT an authorized FedRAMP route in the source material?

  • A. Claude for Government (FedRAMP High via PFCS-SS)
  • B. Claude via Amazon Bedrock GovCloud (High, DoD IL4/5)
  • C. Claude via Vertex AI Assured Workloads
  • D. Claude Enterprise on AWS Marketplace

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: D. Also keep dev/test off the commercial endpoint, since code patterns and credentials leak between environments.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Verify current status at trust.anthropic.com.

questions.promptHtml:
A law firm needs privileged documents processed. What survives review?

  • A. Consumer Claude.ai
  • B. Direct API/SDK calls from the firm's own app via SSO and an approved LLM gateway with full request/response logging implemented at the application layer
  • C. Any endpoint, if the prompt says "confidential"
  • D. Personal API keys

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Conversation content is not captured by Anthropic by default on direct API traffic, so you must log it; confirm the design with the account team.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The firm needs an audited path: direct API or SDK calls from its own application, SSO, an approved LLM gateway, and full request and response logging. Because Anthropic does not capture conversation content by default on direct API traffic, the organization must implement the logging itself. Consumer surfaces cannot be audited end to end, and a prompt wording does not change the endpoint.

questions.contextHtml: A production service called the model through a moving alias. After an upstream update, outputs shifted and a downstream parser broke. There was no eval run and no way to roll back quickly.
questions.promptHtml:
What should the release process include?

  • A. Always use the newest alias
  • B. Pin a model snapshot, promote a new version only through the eval, and retain the prior version for rollback
  • C. Test manually
  • D. Avoid upgrades forever

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blaming the vendor for the change.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in outputs? Which eval cases regressed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin the last known good snapshot.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Alias moved; prompt sensitivity; parser brittleness.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the eval against both versions.
  5. Root cause: A silent production change via an unpinned alias.
  6. Fix: B.
  7. Prevention: Gate promotion on eval scores; keep the previous version deployable.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Pinning adds release overhead; accept it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Which platform? → Usually the customer's cloud; compare latency from their region, compliance and total cost.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the vendor.
  • Hire: pins.
  • Strong hire: pins, gates on eval, retains rollback.

questions.promptHtml:
What comes before choosing a platform?

  • A. Buying credits
  • B. Deriving checkable functional and infrastructure requirements from the business problem and documenting them so the decision can be defended
  • C. Writing the UI
  • D. Picking the biggest model

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Each lifecycle phase should have an artifact and a gate; skipping gates under deadline is the usual failure.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Capture functional requirements from the business problem, then derive infrastructure requirements (residency, identity, latency, volume) before any platform is picked, and document them so the decision is defensible. Each lifecycle phase needs a defined artifact and a gate; gates are what teams under deadline are tempted to skip.

questions.contextHtml: A multi-component Claude application passes data between a retriever, an agent, and a ticketing system. Nobody marked the hand-off between retriever and agent as a boundary; a review stalls.
questions.promptHtml:
What do you do?

  • A. Nothing; internal hops are trusted
  • B. Map components, name every seam as a trust boundary, apply least privilege per component and log boundary crossings
  • C. Merge everything into one component
  • D. Remove logging

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Assuming internal hops are safe.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What data crosses each seam? Who can write to it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add logging at the seams.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Unvalidated content enters the agent; over-broad credentials.
  4. How I'd verify each: Walk the integration map.
  5. Root cause: An unnamed seam.
  6. Fix: B.
  7. Prevention: Include the map in the design doc.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't skip audit work to save time.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Who owns the credential for each component? → Each gets its own, scoped narrowly.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: trusts internal hops.
  • Hire: names boundaries.
  • Strong hire: boundaries plus least privilege plus logging.

questions.promptHtml:
How do you turn a one-off delivery into a reusable asset?

  • A. Zip the repo
  • B. Parameterize while the build is fresh, separate customer-specific from reusable parts, document assumptions and bundle the audit log
  • C. Delete tests
  • D. Hard-code the customer name

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Contributing upstream additionally needs verifiable examples and tests plus a rights/licensing/attribution check before technical review.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: An accelerator keeps reusable parts and separates customer-specific ones while the build is fresh, documents assumptions, and bundles the audit log. To contribute upstream, match the contribution to the right channel, include examples and tests a maintainer can verify, and clear rights, licensing and attribution first.
